extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, patent agents, applicants for USPTO registration, and legal professionals involved with USPTO enrollment/discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures governing who may practice before the USPTO, the registration requirements for practitioners, what activities constitute practice, and the Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) investigation, adjudication, sanctions, and mitigating/aggravating considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration requirements / 3 factors for registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Three factors for registration: Scientific and technical qualifications; Legal competence: registration exam; and Moral character. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.7 and General Requirements Bulletin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the substantive prerequisites to be authorized to practice before the USPTO in patent matters (attorneys, agents, limited recognition). The page cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.7 as the governing provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization categories to practice before the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorization to practice before the USPTO in patent matters includes attorneys, agents, and limited recognition practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different categories have different eligibility pathways and privileges; applicants should consult the General Requirements Bulletin and applicable CFR sections for category-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activities constituting practice before the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the USPTO is broadly defined (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.5(b) and 11.14) and includes communicating with and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the USPTO; consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1)); and consulting with or giving advice in contemplation of filing a trademark application or other document (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition captures pre-filing advice and communications about matters to be presented to the Office. Practitioners must be registered (or otherwise authorized) to perform these activities; reliance on non-registered persons for such advice can trigger discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-practitioner assistants under supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b) proscribes a practitioner from employing or retaining non-practitioner assistants under the supervision of the practitioner to assist in matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervising practitioners remain responsible for work delegated to assistants; proper supervision is required to avoid discipline for unauthorized practice or misconduct by assistants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may practice in trademark and non-patent matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 37 C.F.R. § 11.14 for details regarding individuals who may practice before the USPTO in trademark and other non-patent matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark/non-patent practice has distinct eligibility rules; practitioners should consult § 11.14 to determine permissible activities and qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary jurisdiction of the OED
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary jurisdiction (37 C.F.R. § 11.19) covers all practitioners engaged in practice before the USPTO (e.g., trademark practitioners, pro hac vice in PTAB, those representing others in OED proceedings, etc.) and non-practitioners who engage in or offer to engage in practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdiction extends to registered and certain unregistered actors; offering or engaging in practice can trigger OED authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governing regulations: USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101–11.901) govern practitioner behavior before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules set the substantive conduct standards (conflicts, candor, competence, diligence, confidentiality, etc.) that form the basis for grievances and disciplinary actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance and investigation process
rubrics_metrics.description: OED investigation begins with receipt of a grievance by the OED Director. Grievance: a written submission from any source that presents possible grounds for discipline of a specified practitioner (See 37 C.F.R. § 11.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-reporting is often considered a mitigating factor. After investigation, the OED Director may terminate an investigation with no action, issue a warning, institute formal charges (with Committee on Discipline approval), or enter into a settlement agreement submitted to the USPTO Director for approval (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee on Discipline (COD) referral and adjudication steps
rubrics_metrics.description: OED presents investigation results to the COD; COD determines if probable cause of misconduct exists. If probable cause is found, the Solicitor’s Office (for the OED Director) files a formal complaint with a hearing officer, who issues an initial decision; either party may appeal the initial decision to the USPTO Director, otherwise it becomes final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.22, 11.23, 11.32, 11.34, 11.40, 11.54 and 11.55 for procedural detail. Procedural compliance and timely responses affect outcome and appeal rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available disciplinary sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions include exclusion from practice before the USPTO (minimum of five years, reinstatement only upon petition per §§ 11.58(a), 11.60(a)), suspension for an appropriate period (reinstatement only upon petition upon expiration), reprimand or censure, probation (in lieu of or in addition to other sanctions), and possible conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severity depends on misconduct; exclusion has a statutory minimum and reinstatement requirements. Sanctions may be combined and conditioned on compliance or rehabilitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other discipline mechanisms (reciprocal/interim/exclusion on consent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.24) is based on discipline by a state or federal program or agency and is often conducted on the documentary record only. Interim suspension based on conviction of a serious crime (37 C.F.R. § 11.25) is referred to a hearing officer for determination of final action. Exclusion on Consent (37 C.F.R. § 11.27) is also available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State or federal disciplinary actions can be the basis for USPTO discipline without full re-litigation; criminal convictions can trigger immediate interim measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warnings under 37 C.F.R. § 11.21
rubrics_metrics.description: A warning is neither public nor a disciplinary sanction. The OED Director may conclude an investigation with the issuance of a warning. The warning shall contain a statement of facts and identify the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct relevant to the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A warning will not be an option if a formal complaint has been filed with a hearing officer. Warnings are non-public but document conduct and applicable rules; they may be relied on in future proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disreputable or gross misconduct — examples and rule references
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: submitting unprofessional remarks in Office action responses (stricken under 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(c)(1)); leaving profane voicemails for judges. Such conduct can be outside ordinary professional obligations and client interests and can result in suspension (example default: 6-month suspension). Relevant rules cited include 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) (disreputable or gross misconduct), § 10.89(c)(5) (discourteous conduct before the Office), § 10.23(b)(5) (conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice), and § 11.18 (certification upon filing of papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples show courts consider aggravating factors (e.g., lack of remorse) and may strike filings; sanctions vary with severity. Practitioners must avoid discourteous, prejudicial, or dishonorable conduct and must make truthful certifications on filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating and aggravating factors in sanction determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors include prior unblemished practice, cooperation with OED, expression of remorse, voluntary corrective actions (e.g., counseling), and self-reporting. Aggravating factors include failure to accept responsibility or show remorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in one matter, mitigation (20 years private practice, cooperation, remorse, anger-management counseling) led to reprimand plus conditions rather than suspension; in another, absence of remorse aggravated the sanction (6-month suspension). OED considers history, cooperation, remediation, and candor in assessing discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification upon filing of papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must comply with certification requirements when filing papers (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.18); false or improper certifications can be the basis for disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule supports striking inappropriate remarks and underpins disciplinary findings when filings include unlawful or unprofessional statements; practitioners must ensure accuracy and propriety in certifications.
